Exercise 1.1: Cleaning and Preparing Data with Pandas

























Handle Missing Data

Remove rows

Convert a Column to a Different Data Type and Rename a Column

Convert a Column to a Different Data Type














Rename a Column








Filter a DataFrame



















Common Pitfall: Methods like .dropna() and .fillna() return a new DataFrame and leave the original untouched unless you assign the result back (e.g., populations = populations.dropna()). If your “cleaning” seems to have no effect, check whether you forgot to capture the return value.


Common Pitfall: Filling missing numbers with 0 quietly changes your data’s meaning – a country with a missing GDP is not a country with a GDP of zero. Decide whether dropping, zero-filling, or mean/median-filling is honest for your analysis before you reach for .fillna(0).




Self-Check
By the end of this module, you should be able to:

Load a CSV into a pandas DataFrame and inspect it with .head(), .info(), and .describe()
Handle missing values by dropping rows (.dropna()) or filling them (.fillna()), and explain the tradeoff
Convert a column between data types with .astype() and rename columns with .rename()
Filter rows on a single condition and on multiple conditions combined with & / |
Recognize when a pandas operation returns a new object versus modifying in place

Summary Tables








Analyzing Categorical Data

Using Cross-Tabulation








By Getting Group Counts







Common Pitfall: When you call .agg() or .groupby(...).agg(), make sure you are grouping on the key you actually mean (e.g., continent vs. region). Grouping on the wrong column gives you a perfectly valid-looking table that answers the wrong question.


Common Pitfall: pd.pivot_table() silently averages with aggfunc='mean' by default. If your summary numbers look surprising, confirm which aggregation function is being applied – a “mean of counts” is rarely what you want.




Self-Check
By the end of this module, you should be able to:

Group rows with .groupby() and compute a summary statistic per group
Apply a function element-wise to a column with .map()
Use .agg() to apply different aggregations to different columns
Build a summary grid with pd.pivot_table() and choose its index, columns, and aggfunc
Count categories with pd.crosstab() and .value_counts()

Common Pitfall: Matplotlib draws onto the current figure, so forgetting plt.figure() before a new plot (or forgetting plt.show() after) can cause charts to overlap or render in unexpected places. Start each chart with a fresh plt.figure().


Common Pitfall: A bar chart whose y-axis does not start at 0 visually exaggerates differences. When you set plt.ylim(...), keep the lower bound at 0 for bar charts unless you have a deliberate reason not to.



Self-Check
By the end of this module, you should be able to:

Create line and bar charts (vertical and horizontal) with Matplotlib
Add labels, a title, gridlines, and adjust axis limits and tick marks
Draw a histogram, boxplot, and violin plot with Seaborn
Explain what each chart type reveals about a distribution or comparison
Filter a DataFrame to the rows a chart needs before plotting

section: Two ways to work
text:
Two ways to work


📝 Exercises
The live-coding template. Code cells start mostly empty so you can fill them in as we go. Your edits are saved automatically in this browser, so you can pick up where you left off.


✅ Solutions
The completed code for every walkthrough and exercise. Run any cell to see the output, or edit a cell to experiment with your own variations.

title: GenAI-Powered Data Analysis with Python
section: How it works
text:
How it works

Click Run Code on any code cell to execute it in your browser.
Run the import cell and the data-loading cells near the top of a page first, then work top to bottom — later cells reuse variables from earlier ones.
The first cell you run takes a few seconds while Python and the data packages load. After that it’s fast.
The two datasets — economies.csv and populations.csv — are bundled with the page, so pd.read_csv(...) just works.







NoteNeed the originals?



The Jupyter notebooks, slides, and data are all in the course GitHub repository. You can also run the notebooks on Google Colab if you prefer a full Jupyter environment.








TipBrowser support



The in-browser plots need a modern browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari, kept up to date). If a plot cell shows an OffscreenCanvas error, update your browser to the latest version.

title: Walkthroughs & Exercises — GenAI-Powered Data Analysis with Python
text:
TipHow to use this page





Everything runs in your browser — there’s no Python or Jupyter to install.

Click Run Code on the import cell and the data-loading cells near the top first.
Then work through the page top to bottom, filling in each cell as we live-code together.
Your edits are saved automatically in this browser. Use Start Over on a cell to reset it.
The very first run takes a few seconds while Python loads in the background.

Stuck? Open the completed solutions in another tab.
